source_read: PDF PDFs/Cannabis/Hall_2009_AdverseHealthEffectsLancet.pdf, pp. 1383-1391 (all pages read in a text extraction; pp. 1386-1389, including Panels 1 and 2, checked on rendered pages)

claims.note: This review is cited for one in six with adolescent onset against about 9% of everyone who has used; both figures are cited to a 2006 book chapter (ref 37, Anthony, in Roffman & Stephens, eds), with no diagnostic system, age cut-off for adolescence or adjustment stated. I confirm that the review contains no figure of 25-50% for dependence among people who use daily (full text, panels and conclusions searched); its only daily-use percentages are that about 10% of people who ever use go on to use daily and 20-30% weekly (p. 1383). The claim's statement that the figure Volkow et al. (2014) cite to this review cannot be traced is therefore correct as far as this review goes. For the editor: the same 25-50% figure appears, with no citation on that sentence, in Page et al. (2020, p. e13, Addiction Considerations).

anchors.locator: Health effects of cannabis › Chronic effects, 2nd paragraph (begins at foot of left column; figures in right column)
anchors.extracted: Lifetime risk of dependence among people who have used cannabis estimated at about 9%, rising to one in six among people who start in adolescence; both cited to ref 37 (Anthony, 2006 book chapter). No diagnostic system, age cut-off or adjustment given.

anchors.locator: Health effects of cannabis › Chronic effects, 2nd paragraph (right column)
anchors.extracted: People at highest risk of dependence have a history of poor academic achievement, deviant behaviour in childhood and adolescence, rebelliousness, poor parental relationships, or parental drug and alcohol problems (ref 37): markers other than frequency or age at first use.

In the USA about 10% of people who ever use cannabis go on to use it daily and 20-30% weekly (ref 5). These are the only daily-use percentages in the review; no 25-50% figure for dependence among people who use daily appears anywhere on pp. 1383-1389, Panels 1-2 or the conclusions.

claims.note: Second-hand: the 9% is cited to a 2006 book chapter (ref 37) and the comparison figures to the 1994 National Comorbidity Survey paper (ref 38, Anthony, Warner & Kessler), as the claim says; rounded, they match the claim's survey figures (31.9, 23.1, 16.7 and 15.4%). The review also gives 1-2% of adults with dependence in the past year and 4-8% in their lifetime in Australia, Canada and the USA (refs 5, 37) and 11% for stimulants, neither of which the claim needs. No diagnostic system is named for the 9%. Panel 1 and the conclusions round it to around, and as many as, one in ten.

anchors.locator: Health effects of cannabis › Chronic effects, 2nd paragraph (right column)
anchors.extracted: Dependence affected 1-2% of adults in the past year and 4-8% in their lifetime (Australia, Canada, USA; refs 5, 37). Lifetime risk among people who have used cannabis about 9% (ref 37, 2006 book chapter); equivalent lifetime risks 32% nicotine, 23% heroin, 17% cocaine, 15% alcohol, 11% stimulants (ref 38, National Comorbidity Survey, 1994).

anchors.locator: Panel 1 (chronic adverse effects, 1st bullet); also p. 1389, Conclusions, 2nd paragraph
anchors.extracted: Panel 1 lists a dependence syndrome in around one in ten people who use; the conclusions say chronic use can produce dependence in as many as one in ten.

claims.note: The review relays Mittleman et al. (2001) as 4.8 times the risk of myocardial infarction in the hour after use among 3,882 patients, in causal wording (use can raise the risk) and without an interval or the number of people exposed (the 9 people and the missing interval are documented in Page et al., 2020). It gives the follow-up of 1,913 of these patients as a dose-response with mortality over 3.8 years, 2.5 times with use less than once a week and 4.2 times with use more than once a week, without intervals or significance tests; Page et al. (2020, p. e17) describe the mortality findings of these smaller studies (their refs 37 and 87, Frost 2013 and Mukamal 2008) as a signal of which many did not reach statistical significance, so the magnitude's 2.5 and 4.2 should carry that caution. The heart-rate sentence is cited to two 2002 reviews (refs 56, 57) and the angina sentence to a laboratory study (ref 60).

anchors.locator: Health effects of cannabis › Chronic effects, 7th paragraph (left column; begins 'Evidence exists to support the adverse cardiovascular effects')
anchors.extracted: Cannabis and THC raise heart rate in a dose-dependent way; healthy young adults are marginally affected and quickly develop tolerance; concern about adults with cardiovascular disease (refs 56, 57, both reviews). Laboratory studies indicate that smoking cannabis provokes angina in patients with heart disease (ref 60).

anchors.locator: Health effects of cannabis › Chronic effects, 7th paragraph (left column)
anchors.extracted: Case-crossover study of 3,882 patients with myocardial infarction (ref 58): risk of infarction 4.8 times in the hour after use (no interval, no number exposed). Prospective follow-up of 1,913 of them (ref 59): dose-response with mortality over 3.8 years, 2.5 times with use less than once a week and 4.2 times with use more than once a week (no intervals).

claims.overstatement: Mild: the claim relays the review's causal verb (the earlier meta-analysis 'found that regular cannabis smoking in pregnancy reduced birth weight') for a meta-analysis of observational studies. The review uses a causal verb here (decreased) but a hedged one in its conclusions (could reduce); 'was associated with lower birth weight' would be closer to the evidence if the editors avoid relaying causal verbs.
claims.note: Second-hand (refs 29-31: Zuckerman et al. 1989; Fergusson et al. 2002; English et al. 1997, the meta-analysis). The review also lists the confounders that limit interpretation (co-use of tobacco, alcohol and other illicit drugs; less antenatal care; poorer nutrition), which the claim covers in general terms through Gunn et al.'s caveat.

anchors.locator: Health effects of cannabis › Reproductive effects, 1st paragraph (right column; continues on p. 1386)
anchors.extracted: High doses cause growth retardation and malformations in animals; epidemiological evidence of more birth defects is scarce; the few associations are hard to interpret because women who use cannabis more often use tobacco, alcohol and other illicit drugs in pregnancy, seek antenatal care less and have poorer nutrition (refs 25-28).

anchors.locator: Health effects of cannabis › Reproductive effects, 1st paragraph continued (left column, top)
anchors.extracted: No increased risk of birth defects in a large group of women who used cannabis (Zuckerman et al., ref 29). Reduced birthweight is the most consistent association in large studies (ref 30); a meta-analysis (ref 31) found that regular cannabis smoking in pregnancy decreased birthweight, less than tobacco smoking did, probably through carbon monoxide.
Use during pregnancy could reduce birthweight but does not seem to cause birth defects; whether it contributes to behavioural disorders in the children is uncertain.

claims.note: The claim's text does not cite Hall & Degenhardt (2009). As far as this review goes, the claim is consistent with it: a consistent association with a frequency gradient, attenuated after adjustment, with a common cause not excluded because no study measured all major confounders. If the anchor is kept, the claim's list of how narrative reviews read the evidence could add this one: it lists psychotic symptoms and disorders in people who use heavily among the probable chronic adverse effects (Panel 1), not among the effects whose causal relation is unknown (Panel 2), most probably in people with a personal or family history of psychotic symptoms. Its pooled odds ratios (1.4 and 2.09) are Moore et al. (2007), relayed. It also relays Zammit et al.'s estimate that 13% of schizophrenia cases would be averted without cannabis use, a calculation that assumes causality.

anchors.locator: Cannabis and mental health, 2nd paragraph (right column)
anchors.extracted: Pooled OR 1.4 (95% CI 1.20-1.65) for psychotic symptoms or disorders with ever use, and 2.09 (1.54-2.84) with regular use against no use (Moore et al., ref 87). Reverse causation addressed in most studies by excluding or adjusting for baseline psychotic symptoms; a common cause was difficult to exclude because adjustment for potential confounders attenuated the association and no study assessed all major confounders.

anchors.locator: Cannabis and mental health, 1st paragraph (right column)
anchors.extracted: Swedish conscripts (50,465; 15-year follow-up): 2.4 times as likely to be diagnosed with schizophrenia after trying cannabis by 18; risk rose with frequency; 2.3 times with use 10 or more times by 18 after adjustment for a few confounders. Zammit et al. (27-year follow-up): dose-response persisted after adjustment; 13% of cases could be averted if use were prevented. Cohorts in the Netherlands, Germany and New Zealand: associations persisted after adjustment.

anchors.locator: Panel 1 (chronic adverse effects, 3rd bullet) and Panel 2; also p. 1389, Conclusions, 2nd paragraph
anchors.extracted: Psychotic symptoms and disorders in people who use heavily, especially with a personal or family history, are listed among chronic adverse effects (Panel 1), not among Panel 2's possible effects with unknown causal relation; the conclusions say the strongest mental-health evidence is for psychotic symptoms and disorders.

claims.note: Supports the list as far as this review goes. The Australian study (ref 88) is by the reviewers' own group (Degenhardt, Hall & Lynskey, 2003). The other British study with no increase is cited to the Advisory Council on the Misuse of Drugs 2008 report (ref 92), so it is known only through that report, as the claim says. This review does not call the Australian and English studies modelling studies or the London and Zurich studies case registers, and gives no doubling figure; those details come from the claim's other sources.

anchors.locator: Cannabis and mental health, 3rd paragraph (right column)
anchors.extracted: Evidence conflicting on whether schizophrenia incidence rises as use rises, as expected if the association were causal. Australian study (ref 88): no clear increase in psychosis incidence despite steep rises in use in the 1980s and 1990s. Similar study (ref 89): too early to see an increase in England and Wales in the 1990s. A British (ref 90, south-east London, 1965-1999) and a Swiss study (ref 91, Zurich) reported increases in psychoses in recent birth cohorts; another British study did not (ref 92, government advisory report, 2008).

claims.note: Second-hand. This review gives non-consistent and weak associations, the Fergusson & Horwood result and the meta-analytic OR 1.49 (1.15-1.94) with the meta-analysts' caveat. The Swedish conscript result and the comparison with psychosis (weaker) are in Hall (2015), not here. The OR 1.49 pools longitudinal studies of any age (Moore et al., 2007), not only adolescents, which the claim's wording ('an earlier meta-analysis of longitudinal studies') respects.

anchors.locator: Cannabis and mental health, 4th paragraph (left column)
anchors.extracted: Non-consistent and weak associations with depression. Fergusson & Horwood (ref 93): dose-response between frequency of use at 16 and depressive disorder, not significant after adjustment for confounders. Meta-analysis (ref 87): OR 1.49 (95% CI 1.15-1.94) for depressive disorders; its authors said the studies had not controlled confounders or excluded that depressed young people are more likely to use cannabis.

anchors.locator: Panel 2 (3rd bullet); also p. 1389, Conclusions, 3rd paragraph
anchors.extracted: Depressive disorders, mania and suicide listed among possible adverse effects of regular use whose causal relation is unknown; for depressive disorders and suicide the association with cannabis is uncertain.

claims.note: Editors' calculation recomputed: from 16% and 2% the crude odds ratio is 9.3 (9.1 from the implied counts, 48 of 302 and 21 of 1,028); because the percentages are rounded it could lie between about 7 and 13, so 'about 9' is right. The suicidal-ideation result in males and the depression-but-not-suicide result come from Hall (2015) only. Patton et al. are described here as finding an association in women but not men, matching the claim's 'females only'.

anchors.locator: Cannabis and mental health, 5th paragraph (left column)
anchors.extracted: Case-control studies show a relation between cannabis use and suicide in adolescents; whether causal is unclear. New Zealand case-control study of serious suicide attempts needing hospital care (ref 94): 16% of 302 people who attempted suicide met criteria for cannabis dependence or abuse against 2% of 1,028 community controls; control for social disadvantage, depression and alcohol dependence substantially reduced but did not eliminate the association (OR 2).

anchors.locator: Cannabis and mental health, 6th paragraph (left column)
anchors.extracted: Prospective evidence mixed: dose-response between frequency of use at 16 and self-reported suicide attempt did not persist after adjustment (ref 93); cannabis associated with self-harm in women but not men after controlling for depression and alcohol use (Patton et al., ref 95); a meta-analysis (ref 87) found the studies too heterogeneous to estimate risk, few having excluded reverse causation or controlled confounding.

claims.overstatement: Mild, attribution: the claim says people seeking help to stop 'most often' report anxiety, sleep problems, appetite disturbance and low mood, citing this review. Hall & Degenhardt (2009) lists these among the withdrawal symptoms such people report, without ranking them; the ranking (most common) is in Hall (2015, p. 5), which the claim cites in the next clause. Citing Hall (2015), or both, for that sentence would fix it.
claims.note: Second-hand (ref 40, Budney & Hughes, 2006). The same paragraph notes tolerance in animals and humans, and that a cannabinoid antagonist precipitates a withdrawal syndrome in rats, mice and dogs that THC reverses (animal evidence, ref 39).

anchors.locator: Health effects of cannabis › Chronic effects, 3rd paragraph (right column)
anchors.extracted: Animals and humans develop tolerance to many effects of THC; the antagonist SR141716A causes a withdrawal syndrome in rats, mice and dogs that THC reverses (ref 39). People seeking help to stop report withdrawal symptoms that include anxiety, insomnia, appetite disturbance and depression (ref 40). Rising numbers seek help in the USA, Europe and Australia; after cognitive-behavioural therapy only 15% remain abstinent 6-12 months after treatment.

key_findings.note: Locators checked on the rendered p. 1383: the definition sentence closes the 3rd paragraph of Pattern of cannabis use at the top of the right column.

Worth adding here: these are the review's only daily-use percentages; it contains no 25-50% figure for dependence among people who use daily, although Volkow et al. (2014) cite it for one (see missed).

Worth adding: the review gives no interval, number of people exposed or significance test for 4.8, 2.5 or 4.2. Page et al. (2020, p. e17) report that 9 patients had used within the hour, and that many mortality findings of these smaller studies (Frost 2013; Mukamal 2008) were not statistically significant.
Editors' calculation recomputed: 9.3 from the percentages (9.1 from the implied counts 48/302 and 21/1,028); with rounded percentages it could lie between about 7 and 13.

The card leaves out the paragraph's uncited sentence that respiratory and cardiovascular effects could be reduced if people adjusted their THC intake and smoked less; leaving it out is right under the no-advice rule, and it is speculation in any case.

reporting_issues.note: Printed as 5 and 1 μg/mL on p. 1385.

Hall & Degenhardt word it as following up children born to 655 women in Pittsburgh between 1990 and 1995, which could mean birth years or follow-up years; either reading is impossible for a 1994 paper. Hall (2015, p. 4) says the children were born between 1990 and 1995.

Slightly strong as worded: the body does offer one positive cohort finding (impaired respiratory function at 26 in people dependent on cannabis, not replicated) and impaired respiratory immune competence, so 'weakly supported' is more exact than 'not supported'. The consequence stands.

Correction: the dose qualifier does appear in the body, as an uncited statement in the potency paragraph (p. 1389: high THC content can increase psychotic symptoms in people new to cannabis), though not in the acute-effects text, which links psychotic symptoms to inexperience. The 10-year threshold has no basis in the body beyond the Yücel et al. sample. The consequence stands: neither qualifier rests on evidence presented in the review.

risk_of_bias.note: Domain facts checked: 5 of 96 references have an author of the review (refs 2, 5, 68, 77, 88); refs 18 and 48 are chapters in a book Hall co-edited; a rough count of superscripts in the text extraction gives about 18 citations of ref 5 and 9 of ref 9, as the card says. Overall high follows the worst domain.

interpretation_gap.note: Substantial: the Summary and Panel 1 go beyond the body (respiratory function, history qualifiers, the 10-year threshold) and the Summary's cardiovascular statement is not carried into the panels or conclusions; the conclusions are measured on causation.

missed: No figure of 25-50% for dependence among people who use daily appears anywhere in the review (text, panels, conclusions), although Volkow et al. (2014) cite this review for one (used in cl_can_dependence_frequency_onset). The card should say so under KF 3 or KF 8 so that the figure is not traced back here. The same figure appears, with no citation on the sentence, in Page et al. (2020, p. e13).

Withdrawal (KF 9): the review lists anxiety, insomnia, appetite disturbance and depression among the symptoms people seeking help report, without ranking them; the ranking 'most common' is Hall (2015, p. 5). Relevant because cl_can_withdrawal attributes 'most often' to this review.
